citation.title: Effect of disclosing AI-generated content on prosocial advertising evaluation

reading.source_scope_note: Three US online-panel studies compare source labels on identical AI-generated charitable-ad images. Credibility and ad attitudes are human self-reports; Study3 uses donation choices with a20% chance of implementation. Human-likeness is a measured post-exposure moderator, not randomized. Statistical mediation and proposed persuasion-knowledge activation are not established causal mechanisms.
access_limits: All supplied article pages and image-only stimulus content read visually. No additional supplement was obtained after publisher HTML returned403. Data are available on reasonable author request; no author contacted and no participant-level data/code obtained.
Exact condition Ns, exclusion/recruitment flow, preregistration, manipulation checks, raw donation records and realized participant-level transfers are not supplied. No claim to have verified them.
Friestad/Wright1994, Isaac/Grayson, Giroux and other original cited experiments/books are not independently fully read. Metadata/selected-abstract consultations are not separate full-paper credits.

Group mean/SD inconsistencies cannot be repaired by guessing a scale, decimal shift or replacement statistic. Source identity and construct definitions remain usable without endorsing every empirical claim.

study.samples: Study1 N226 CloudResearchConnect,mean age39.68,50.4%female; Study2 N360 MTurk,42.64,51.7%female; Study3 N180 MTurk,42.00,46.7%female. Total766 sample participations, not verified unique people across panels. AllUS, compensated; no representative population sampling.
study.study1: Random disclosure versus no-disclosure conditions on the same DALL·E3 image of a child. AppendixA adds an AI disclaimer in one condition; absence of that label is not a verified human-source claim. Credibility uses credible/trustworthy items; ad attitude bad/negative/unfavorable items on seven-point scales.
study.study2: Same generated elephant/WWF image labeled AI versus professional wildlife photographer, rather than disclosure versus silence. Method describes a2×2 high/low design but actually analyzes continuous0–100 perceived AI human-likeness measured after the credibility/attitude outcomes. No randomized humanization factor; professional expertise and captured-versus-generated framing accompany source identity.
study.stimulus_check: AppendixB human label says Captured by a professional wildlife photographer, while Methods paraphrase Generated by a professional wildlife photographer. Both conditions use the AI-generated image. This is an experimental source-label contrast, not a comparison of genuinely human/AI content quality; debriefing details are not supplied.
study.study2_results: Formal disclosure×continuous-human-likeness interactions are reported for credibility and attitude, eachB.014, with nonzeroCIs. A formal Model7 moderated-mediation index.011[.003,.019] is also reported. Human-like perception attenuates but does not eliminate the negative contrast: credibility differences about1.38/.60 and attitude1.26/.54 at±1SD. Do not infer moderation merely from separate significance or claim it was untested.
study.study3: Randomized label comparison withN180. Participants allocate0–2 dollars of a possible bonus;36 randomly selected participants have the bonus/donation mechanism implemented. Choices therefore have potential real consequences, not purely hypothetical intentions, but not all180 are observed realized transfers. Actual donated total and participant-level implementation are not reported.
study.mediation: Studies1/3 use Model4 with5000 bootstrap draws; Study2 uses measured moderation/conditional indirect effects. Disclosure is randomized but credibility is measured, not independently manipulated. Post-exposure human-likeness can itself depend on treatment. These models do not establish unique causal credibility or persuasion-knowledge pathways, nor full mediation merely because cprime is nonsignificant.
study.reporting_limits: Study1 attitudeF36.72,df1/224 implies partialeta.14084, not.03; it also exceeds a conservative6.48 upper bound from rounded means/SDs andN226. Study3 human-conditionmean1.61/SD1.35 is incompatible with a0–2 scale even allowing n=2 sample correction and rounding. AI-conditionSD1.32 is incompatible with itsmean1.20 for any n>=3. No repaired values or fraud claim.
study.counterevidence: The literature review acknowledges neutral/positive disclosure results in other contexts. No direct commercial-versus-charitable comparison or cross-cultural generality tested. Authors explicitly recommend ongoing transparency/education and reject selective omission of disclosures.

study1_attitude.interpretation: Reported F is inconsistent with the stated eta and rounded means/SDs; no replacement F inferred.

study3_human_donation.interpretation: Even the n=2 finite-sample correction and rounding cannot reconcile human-condition mean/SD with a0–2 scale.

study3_AI_donation.interpretation: AI-condition SD also exceeds the bounded-score maximum for any n>=3; condition Ns are not printed.

study1_mediation.interpretation: Mediation coefficients are broadly compatible with rounding; do not declare them inconsistent because the separate F statistic is problematic.

summary: Add persuasion knowledge as an explicitly secondary theoretical construct and perceived credibility as a measured human appraisal. Enrich anthropomorphism/algorithm aversion without duplicating human-likeness or disclosure labels. Preserve random-implementation donation incentives, formal moderation tests, measured-mediator limits, verified version dates and unresolved statistic/scale inconsistencies.

findings.definition: Knowledge about the goals and tactics of attempts to influence one’s judgments and ways to respond to them.
findings.ai_evidence_status: Secondary theoretical framework; activation not directly measured here and AI analogue untested
findings.novelty_rationale: An interpretive resource for recognizing and coping with influence attempts, distinct from simply rejecting an algorithm, feeling reactance or showing a persuasion backfire. The article explains the construct and allows knowledge to support either greater skepticism or increased credibility.

evidence.quote: how consumers cope with these efforts to influence their decisions
accessing persuasion knowledge can increase perceptions

findings.evidence_scope: The paper applies the persuasion knowledge model to AI-source disclosures. Its experiments measure credibility, attitudes, human-likeness and donation choices, not persuasion knowledge itself; the proposed activation mechanism remains theoretical and original sources are not independently read.
findings.boundary: Recognizing persuasion does not prove manipulation, falsehood, justified rejection or a uniquely identified defense mechanism. Knowledge can help accept a sound argument. Do not equate every disclosure penalty with resistance or assume a model has a human motive-detector or subjective suspicion.
findings.ai_proposal: Test whether an agent identifies supported influence goals/tactics in matched messages, distinguishes those from message truth and source expertise, and evaluates arguments on evidence. Include legitimate persuasive requests and irrelevant influence cues so recognizing a tactic does not become automatic rejection.

findings.definition: Judging a message or source as believable, trustworthy or reliable.
findings.ai_evidence_status: Human message/source appraisal measured; AI-as-evaluator analogue untested
findings.novelty_rationale: A subjective credibility judgment differs from actual accuracy, general moral endorsement, an algorithm’s institutional authority, explainability or an unfair identity-based testimonial deficit. The construct is explicitly defined and directly measured here.

evidence.quote: subjective judgement of a message or source as trustworthy
rated ad credibility using a semantic differential scale

findings.evidence_scope: Credible/trustworthy ratings are lower under AI labels in the reported charitable-image tasks, with measured conditional effects and indirect-effect models. Statistical mediation does not prove a causal psychological pathway, and disputed attitude/donation statistics constrain downstream inferences.
findings.boundary: Credibility can be warranted or misplaced. Source labels, professional credentials, content quality, actual truth and ethical adequacy differ. Lower belief in one synthetic ad is not automatically irrational algorithm aversion or testimonial injustice; ratings do not validate a real charity’s claims.
findings.ai_proposal: Hold message evidence fixed while varying a disclosed source label or credential, then measure confidence and reliance. Compare against independently verified accuracy and relevant expertise; accept justified source-quality differences while detecting unsupported label-based credibility changes.

findings.definition: Attributing human characteristics, intentions, emotions or other mental states to a nonhuman entity.
findings.novelty_rationale: Existing human source-perception construct; add experimental context and inference limits rather than a new disclosure-effect synonym.

evidence.quote: subjective judgement of the extent to

findings.evidence_scope: A single0–100 machine-like/human-like appraisal is measured after ad credibility/attitude. Formal interaction and moderated-mediation results relate it to the disclosure contrast. This enriches existing anthropomorphic perception rather than creating a near-synonymous record.
findings.boundary: Measured post-treatment human-likeness is not a randomized humanization intervention or actual AI mentality. Expertise/source-label confounds and possible treatment effects on the moderator constrain causality; attenuation does not show elimination or universal benefit.

findings.definition: Reluctance to use or accept algorithmic judgments or decisions relative to human judgment in a comparable task.
findings.novelty_rationale: Existing human source-perception construct; add experimental context and inference limits rather than a new disclosure-effect synonym.

evidence.quote: lower levels of perceived ad credibility

findings.evidence_scope: The paper frames negative AI-label reactions through algorithm aversion. Study1 contrasts disclosure with silence; Studies2/3 contrast AI with a professional-photographer attribution for the same generated image. These are source-label effects rather than verified comparisons of content capability.
findings.boundary: Skepticism can be appropriate. Source identity, professional expertise and deception concerns are not isolated, so a penalty alone does not prove irrational distrust or a unique aversion mechanism. Downstream donation statistics have unresolved reporting limits.

findings.definition: A persuasive message shifts the recipient's judgment away from the position it advocates.
findings.novelty_rationale: Existing human source-perception construct; add experimental context and inference limits rather than a new disclosure-effect synonym.
findings.evidence_scope: Negative reactions to a source label concern ad evaluation. The study is not a matched no-message test of movement away from an advocated position.
findings.boundary: Lower ad credibility or donation relative to another label is not automatically backfire. This clarification supplies no new independent backfire paper credit.

unresolved_source_discrepancies.location: PDF9, Study1 ad attitude F/effect size
unresolved_source_discrepancies.finding: F(1,224)=36.72 implies partialeta.14084 rather than.03 and is incompatible with the reported3.33/3.85 means and1.57/1.66 SDs under a standard two-group ANOVA. Even a conservative rounding-aware bound isF<=6.48. An intended replacement statistic cannot be reconstructed safely. Figure1 path arithmetic is broadly compatible with rounding and is not declared wrong merely because this separate F is inconsistent.

For values in[0,2], unbiased sample variance cannot exceed n/(n−1)*mean*(2−mean). Humanmean1.61/SD1.35 violates even the maximum n=2 bound:variance1.8225>1.2558; rounding cannot reconcile it. AImean1.20/SD1.32 violates the bound for any n>=3. Confirm scoring, units, Ns and original output; do not invent a corrected scale or SD.
Displayed means5.62−4.24 give1.38, while prose saysdelta1.36. Preserve displayed means and flag the arithmetic discrepancy rather than changing unknown raw conditional estimates.

Topic knowledge is described as beliefs about manipulative motives, while secondary descriptions of the original model use beliefs about the message’s subject matter. Original model full text was not obtained, so do not promulgate the narrow motive definition as settled or create a separate topic-knowledge record pending primary review.

source_identity_checks.finding: Crossref confirms online11 September2024 and print2 January2026,volume45,issue1,pages171–192. Both dates are legitimate; citation uses the final2026 issue while the supplied advance-PDF evidence locators remain1–22.
Crossref verifies Marian Friestad and Peter Wright1994,Journal of Consumer Research21(1),1–31,DOI10.1086/209380. Identity verification is not independent full-reading credit.

methodological_limits: SelectedUS online panels, two synthetic-image ad stimuli and different label contrasts limit generalization to real campaigns, other media or countries.

Random source-label assignment does not randomize credibility or post-exposure human-likeness. Formal moderation/conditional indirect tests exist but do not by themselves establish causal humanization or persuasion-knowledge activation.
Professional wildlife credentials and captured/generated framing accompany the AI/human label contrast. Same-image stimuli do not compare actual human/AI quality.
Study3 uses incentivized donation choices with36 random implementations; do not call all responses purely hypothetical or all180 observed realized donations.
Bounded donation SDs and a Study1 F/effect-size conflict require original output. No fabricated repaired statistics or wrongdoing allegation.

Authors acknowledge mixed prior disclosure effects and explicitly oppose selectively withholding labels. Lower persuasive effectiveness does not justify deception or establish that transparency is ethically undesirable.

cross_paper_learning.finding: Check bounded-score variance and figure/text consistency, while distinguishing verified reporting problems from guessed repairs. Here incentives are real for randomly selected participants, unlike treating every donation choice as merely hypothetical.
Perceived human-likeness is an attribution, not actual mentality. A one-item rating and conditional association do not settle consciousness or universal dimensions of mind.
Intentions, choice commitments and realized actions differ. Random-implementation incentives add consequences here, but participant-level realized transfers are still not provided.

deferred.term: Separate AI human-likeness / disclosure penalty records
deferred.reason: Human-likeness refines anthropomorphism; disclosure reactions are contextual evidence for existing source/algorithm appraisal rather than a new universal mechanism.

deferred.term: Agent knowledge / topic knowledge / advertising skepticism
deferred.reason: Subcomponents or possible responses in the theoretical framework, not separately measured here. Keep under persuasion knowledge; resolve the topic-definition discrepancy with original text first.

deferred.term: Causal credibility mediation / anthropomorphism-based donation increase
deferred.reason: Measured mediation/moderation does not identify the causal mechanism, and disputed donation summaries constrain effect claims. No added mechanism record or automatic ethical/harm edges.

limitations: Two new human constructs; persuasion knowledge is theoretical background and perceived credibility is directly rated. No unread-original credits, fabricated yearly counts, inferred machine feelings or generalized recommendation to hide AI labels.
